work.title: Homilia in divini corporis sepulturam (in sabbato magno)

paragraphs.text: Where now, you lawless ones, are the commotions, the shouting and the uproar against Christ of a little while ago? Where are the mobs, the plots, the ranks, the weapons and the spears? Where are the kings and priests, and the judges who now stand condemned? Where are the torches and swords and the disorderly clamour? Where are the crowds, the insolence and the shameless din? Truly, truly the peoples have devised empty and vain things. They stumbled against Christ the cornerstone, but it was they who were crushed. They dashed against the solid rock, but they themselves were shattered, and their waves broke up into foam. They struck against the unbreakable anvil, and they themselves were broken to pieces. They lifted up on the wood the Rock of life, and it came down and killed them. They bound the great [?] … and he raised from Hades those who had slept from ages past. [?] … Let us come to know [?] of God hidden beneath the earth [?]

… [?] fulfils: how the Old has grown old, how the New is confirmed, how the ancient things have passed away and how the new have blossomed. At the time of Christ's passion two peoples were present in Zion, one from the Jews and one from the Gentiles; two kings, Pilate and Herod; two high priests, Annas and Caiaphas, so that the two Passovers might take place together, the one coming to an end and the other, Christ's, beginning. Two sacrifices were offered on that same evening, because two salvations, I mean of the living and of the dead, were being wrought. The Jew bound a lamb to sacrifice it for slaughter; the Gentile bound God in the flesh. The one gazed at the shadow; the other ran to God, the Sun [?]. Those who bound Christ sent him away, but those from the Gentiles received him eagerly. The ones offered a sacrifice of beasts, the others a sacrifice that was God's own body. The Jews commemorated the crossing out of Egypt, while the Gentiles were proclaimed in advance the redemption from error. And where did this happen? In Zion, the city of the great King, where salvation was wrought in the midst of the earth. Jesus, the divine child, was made known between two living creatures: between the Father and the Spirit, the two living ones, he was made known as living, life from life, as it says. He was born in the manger between angels and human beings. He was laid as the cornerstone between two peoples. He was proclaimed between the Law and the Prophets together. He was seen on the mountain between Moses and Elijah. Between the two thieves he was made known as God to the grateful thief. Between the present life and the life to come he sits as eternal judge. And today, between the living and the dead, he has wrought a twofold life and salvation. A twofold life, I say again: a twofold birth, birth and rebirth together. So hear the events of Christ's twofold birth and hold fast to its wonders. An angel brought Mary the good news of Christ's birth from his mother; an angel brought Mary Magdalene the good news of his awesome rebirth from the tomb. By night Christ is born in Bethlehem; by night again in [Variant readings: (81) “binds fast”; “in slaughter”; (82) “received”; (83) “hear explicitly” [?].]

Zion he is born again. At his birth he accepts swaddling bands; here too he is wrapped in bands. When he was born he received myrrh; at his burial too he receives myrrh and aloes. There Joseph, a husband who was no husband, is called the husband of Mary; but here Joseph of Arimathea is revealed as the one who buries our Life. In Bethlehem the place was a manger; and in the tomb too the place is like a manger. Shepherds were the first of all to spread the good news of Christ's birth; and shepherds, Christ's disciples, were the first of all to receive the good news of Christ's rebirth from the dead. There the angel cried “Hail!” to the Virgin; and here Christ, the Angel of great counsel, cried out “Hail!” to the women. At his first birth Christ, after forty days, went into the earthly Jerusalem, into the temple, and as the firstborn offered a pair of turtledoves to God. And at his resurrection from the dead Christ, after forty days, went up into the Jerusalem above, from which he had never been separated, and into the true Holy of Holies, as the incorruptible firstborn from the dead, and offered to God the Father, as two spotless turtledoves, our soul and our flesh. And God the Father, the Ancient of Days, received him like a Simeon, as if in his arms, in his own bosom, which nothing can circumscribe. If you hear these things as myths and not with faith, the unbroken seals of the Lord's tomb of Christ's rebirth accuse you. For just as Christ was born of the Virgin while the bolts of virgin nature, wholly intact, that open the womb remained sealed, so Christ's rebirth was accomplished while the seals of the tomb stayed unopened. Let us hear from the holy oracles how, when and by whom Christ our Life is laid in the tomb. “When evening had come,” it says, “there came a rich man named Joseph. He went in boldly to Pilate and asked him for the body of Jesus.” A mortal went in to a mortal, asking to receive God, the God of mortals. Clay asks of clay to receive the Maker of all; grass asks of grass to obtain the heavenly fire; a wretched drop receives the abyss from a wretched drop. Who has seen, who has ever heard of such a thing? A man [gives] to a man the Maker [Variant readings: (86) “the clay” [?]; (87) “small”.]

rich, for he carried a purse full of the treasure of the Godhead. How is he not rich who has acquired the life and salvation of the world? How is Joseph not rich, when he has received as a gift the One who feeds all and rules all? “When evening had come”: for the Sun of righteousness had now set in Hades. And so “there came a rich man named Joseph, from Arimathea,” who had been in hiding for fear of the Jews. “And Nicodemus also came, the one who had come to Jesus by night.” A hidden mystery of mysteries! Two hidden disciples come to hide Jesus in the tomb, and by their own hiddenness they teach the mystery hidden in Hades of the God hidden in the flesh. Each outdid the other in devotion to Christ: Nicodemus was generous with the myrrh and aloes, and Joseph deserves praise for his daring and boldness before Pilate. Casting off all fear, he went in boldly to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus; and having gone in, he acted with great wisdom so as to reach the goal he longed for. He did not use any boasts or lofty words with Pilate, for fear of enraging him and failing in his request. He does not say to him, “Give me the body of Jesus, who a little while ago darkened the sun, split the rocks, shook the earth, opened the tombs and tore the veil of the temple.” He says nothing of the kind to Pilate. Instead [?] he makes a pitiful request, one that seemed small to everyone: “O judge, I have come to ask of you a very small thing.” And so: “Give me a dead man for burial: the body of that Jesus of Nazareth whom you condemned, Jesus the poor, Jesus the homeless, Jesus the hanged, the naked, [?] the worthless, Jesus the carpenter's son, Jesus the prisoner, the one left out under the open sky, the stranger, unknown in his sojourning, the despised, hanged before all. Give me this stranger, for what good is the body of this stranger to you? Give me this stranger, for he came here from a far country to save the stranger; he came down into the dark [land] to bring the stranger up. Give me this stranger, for he alone is truly a stranger. Give me this stranger, whose country we strangers do not know. Give me this stranger, whose father we strangers do not know. Give me this stranger, whose place and birth and manner of life we strangers do not know. Give me this stranger, who lived a strange life and existence in strange lands. Give me this Nazarene stranger [whose birth and manner of life we strangers do not know. Give me this willing stranger], who has nowhere here to lay his head. Give me this stranger [Variant readings: (90) “full of the treasure”; (91) “hiding”; (92) “mysteries” and “hidden”; (93) “surpassed”; (94) “elegant”.]

who, a homeless stranger in a strange land, was born in a manger. Give me this stranger, who straight from the manger fled from Herod as a stranger. Give me this stranger, who from his very swaddling bands was a stranger in Egypt, having no city, no village, no house, no dwelling, no kinsman: this stranger lives in a foreign land. Give me, O governor, this man who hangs naked on the wood, so that I may cover the one who covered the nakedness of my nature. Give me this dead man who is also God, so that I may cover the one who covered my iniquities. Give me, O governor, the dead man who buried my sin in the Jordan. I plead for a dead man wronged by all, sold by a friend, betrayed by a disciple, persecuted by his brothers and struck by a slave. I intercede for a dead man condemned by those whom he had freed from slavery, given vinegar to drink by [?] those to whom he had given drink, wounded by those he had healed, abandoned by his disciples and deprived even of his mother. I implore you, O governor, for a dead man who hangs homeless on the wood. For he has no father here on earth, no friend, no disciple, no kinsman, no one to bury him; he alone is the only-begotten of the Only One, God in the world, and there is no one else.” When Joseph had said these things to Pilate, Pilate ordered that the all-holy body of Jesus be given to him. And he came to the place called Golgotha, took God in the flesh down from the wood and laid him on the ground: God in the flesh, naked, and not a mere man. He who draws all upward is seen lying below. The Life and Breath of all becomes breathless for a short while. He who created the many-eyed creatures is seen sightless. The Resurrection of all lies on his back. God, who raises the dead, dies in the flesh. The thunder of God the Word falls silent for a short while. He who holds the earth in his fist is lifted in human palms. Tell me, Joseph, now that you have asked and received, do you know whom you have taken? Now that you have approached the cross and taken Jesus down, do you know whom you have carried? If you truly know whom you hold, you have now become rich. But how then do you perform this most awe-inspiring burial of Jesus' divine body? Your longing deserves praise, but the disposition of your soul deserves more. Tell me, do you not shudder as you carry in your hands him at whom the cherubim shudder? With what fear indeed [Variant readings: (99) [?] “country … having a mother”; (1) “by his own slaves”; (2) “God, not naked”; (3) [?].]

do you bind, as is done for the dead, the feet of him who gave the power to walk to motionless feet? Do you lift on a bier the one who commanded the paralytic, “Take up your bed and walk”? Do you pour out ointments on the heavenly Ointment, who emptied himself and sanctified the world? Do you dare to wipe that divine side of Jesus, still flowing with blood, the side of the God who healed the woman with the flow of blood? Do you wash with water the body of God, who washed all clean and gave purification? What lamps will you light for the true Light, who enlightens every human being? What funeral songs will you sing to him who is praised without ceasing by the whole heavenly host? Do you shed tears as for a dead man over him who wept and raised Lazarus, four days dead? Do you lament for him who gives joy to all and dispelled Eve's grief? Even so, I call your hands blessed, Joseph, which served and touched the divine hands and feet of Jesus still flowing with blood. I call your hands blessed, which came near the bleeding side of God before Thomas did, the faithful unbeliever, the inquisitive one who is praised. I call your mouth blessed, which was filled insatiably and joined to Jesus' mouth, and was filled from it with the Holy Spirit. I call your eyes blessed, which were laid against Jesus' eyes and received from them the true light. I call your face blessed, which drew near to the face of God. I call your shoulders blessed, which carried the One who carries all. I call your head blessed, which Jesus, the head of all, drew near to. I call your hands blessed, with which you carried him who carries all things. I call Joseph and Nicodemus blessed. For before the cherubim they became those who lifted up and bore God upon themselves; before the six-winged seraphim they became God's ministers, covering and honouring the Lord not with wings but with linen. He at whom the cherubim tremble is carried on the shoulders of Joseph and Nicodemus, and all the ranks of bodiless beings are amazed. For Joseph and Nicodemus came, and so the whole godly people of the angels ran together with them: the cherubim go before, the seraphim run alongside, the thrones help carry, the six-winged ones cover, the many-eyed ones shudder as they see Jesus sightless in the flesh, the powers help cover him, the principalities sing, the ranks tremble, and all the hosts of the heavenly orders are astonished. Bewildered, they ask one another, “What is this fearful word, this fear and trembling, this mystery? What is this great, extraordinary and incomprehensible sight? He who above, to us bodiless beings, is God unclothed [in flesh] and cannot be seen, is below, to mortals, naked and easily seen. [Variant readings: (6) “to himself”; “himself”; (7) read “unapproachable”; (8–9) read “filled” and “joined”; (10) “all things” [?].]

He before whom the cherubim stand in reverence is buried by Joseph and Nicodemus without fear. When did he come down who never left the things above? How did he go out who is within? How did he come to earth who fills all things? How did he put off [his body] unnoticed by all? He who is above with the Father as God, lacking nothing, is below with his mother as a mortal, [truly] lacking nothing. He who never appeared to us, how does he appear to human beings as a man and at the same time as God who loves mankind? How was the invisible seen? How did the immaterial become flesh? How did the one who cannot suffer suffer? How did the Judge stand before a court? How did Life taste death? How is the one who cannot be contained contained in a tomb? How does he dwell in a sepulchre who has not left the Father's bosom? How does he enter the opening of a cave, he who opened the gates of paradise; who did not break open the gates of the Virgin but shattered the gates of Hades; who did not open the doors for Thomas but threw open the gates of the kingdom to human beings, and yet keeps the doors and seals of the tomb unopened? How is he counted among the dead who is free among the dead? How does the Light that knows no evening come into darkness and the shadow of death? Where is he going? Where does he arrive, he who cannot be held by death? What is the reason, the manner, the purpose of his descent into Hades? Perhaps he goes down to bring up Adam, the condemned one, our fellow servant. Truly he goes to seek the first-formed man as a lost sheep. Surely he wishes also to visit those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death. Surely God goes to free captive Adam and Eve, his fellow captive, from their pains, he who is also her son [and therefore has also been shown to be his son]. Come, let us go down with him, let us dance with him, let us hurry, let us leap for joy with him, let us escort him, let us sing hymns, let us make haste, as we behold God's reconciliation with human beings and the release of the condemned granted by a good Master. For he who by nature loves mankind goes with courage and great authority to lead out those bound from ages past, those who dwell in tombs, whom bitter and insatiable death swallowed up like a tyrant, ruling over them, stealing them from God's [number?] [?] and heaping them up; he goes to set them free and number them with those who dwell above. There lies Adam in bonds, the first-formed and first-born of all, [?] the lowest [Variant readings: (14) “all things”; (15) “of heaven”; (16) “awe”; (17) “whom tyrannically” [?].]

[?] type, once made above by Abraham. There is Jacob, grieving in Hades below, who once grieved above because of Joseph. There is Joseph the prisoner, who in the prison in Egypt became, as a type of Christ, both prisoner and master. There is Moses in darkness below, who once lay in darkness above in the basket. There is Daniel in the pit of Hades, who once was in the lions' den above. There is Jeremiah, as in the pit of mire, in the pit of Hades and of the corruption of death. There, in the world-swallowing sea monster of Hades, lies Jonah, a type of Christ, the eternal and pre-eternal Jonah, who lives for ever and to the ages of ages [and beyond]. And there too is David, the ancestor of God, from whom Christ came according to the flesh. But why do I speak of David and Jonah and Solomon? There too is the great John himself, the greatest of all the prophets, proclaiming Christ in advance to all in Hades, as he did from the dark womb: the twofold forerunner, herald to the living and the dead, sent from Herod's prison to the universal prison of Hades, [where] lie the righteous and the unrighteous who had fallen asleep from ages past. And the prophets and all the righteous offered unceasing prayers to God from there in secret, asking for redemption from that endless, gloomy, dark night of pain under the enemy's rule. One said to God, “Out of the belly of Hades hear my cry, my voice”; another, “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice”; another, “Show us your face, and we shall be saved”; another, “You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth”; another, “Stir up your power and come to save us”; another, “Let your compassion come swiftly to meet us, O Lord”; another, “Deliver my soul from the lowest Hades”; another, “Lord, bring my soul up from Hades”; another, “Do not abandon my soul to Hades”; and another, “Let my life rise up from corruption to you, O Lord my God.” Christ, the all-compassionate God, heard them all, and judged it not right to share his loving-kindness only with those who lived in his time and after him, but also with those held in Hades before his coming, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. So God the Word visited human beings in the flesh through ensouled flesh, but to souls set free from their bodies he appeared in Hades through his divine and spotless soul, which was separated from the body but not from the Godhead. Let us then hasten in mind and make our way to Hades, so that we may see how there he mightily overpowers the mighty one, mighty in his might, the tyrant of might; and with all his host, by his lightning, without hands

subdues those deathless ranks of the phalanxes. Christ, the Door, took away the doorless doors and with the wood of the cross broke the gates that are not of wood; with the divine nails he crushed and shattered the everlasting bars; with the bonds of his divine hands he melted the unbreakable chains like wax; and with the spear that pierced God's side he pierced the bodiless heart of the tyrant. There he broke the strength of the bows, when on the cross, like an archer, he stretched out the strings of his divine hands [?]. So if you follow Christ quietly, you will now see where he bound the tyrant and where he hung up his head; how he dug up the prison and where he led out the prisoners; how he trampled the serpent and where he hung up its head; how he freed Adam and raised Eve, how he broke down the dividing wall, how he condemned the bitter dragon and how he set up his unconquerable trophies; where he put death to death, how he destroyed corruption, and where he restored humanity to its ancient dignity. He who yesterday, for the sake of the divine plan, declined the legions of angels and said to Peter, “Do you think I cannot at once summon more than twelve legions of angels?”, today goes down below into Hades and death, in a manner befitting God, both as a warrior and as Lord; and [he overthrows] the tyrant through death, having with him not a mere twelve legions but ten thousand times ten thousand and thousands upon thousands of the deathless armies and invisible ranks of bodiless beings: angels, authorities, thrones without thrones, the six-winged and the wingless, the many-eyed and the eyeless, the heavenly orders. They escort Christ, guard him and honour him as their own Master and King, not as allies; far from it! For what alliance does the almighty Christ need? Rather, as those who are both bound and glad always to stand beside their own Master and God, they are trustworthy bodyguards, armed men and splendid sceptre-bearers of the divine lordly sovereignty, swift, at a mere nod outrunning one another with zeal and divine speed, carrying out the deed at his command, and crowned with victory against the battle lines of enemies and lawless ones. And so, descending then in swift courses and running together with their God and Master to the regions of Hades beneath the earth, and

…a bright, lion-like voice against the opposing powers, and says: “Lift up the gates, O you rulers of yours!” After him Michael too cries out: “And be lifted up, you everlasting gates!” Then the powers also say: “Stand aside, you lawless gatekeepers!” Then authority after authority: “Be shattered, you unbreakable chains!” And another: “Be put to shame, you hostile enemies!” And another: “Be afraid, you lawless tyrants!” When some fearsome, invincible, all-powerful and triumphant royal army is drawn up for battle, a shuddering, a turmoil and an anguished fear fall upon the enemies of its unconquerable Master. In just this way a sudden terror came upon those in Hades at the unexpected coming of Christ into the regions beneath the earth. A darkening flash of lightning from above blinded the eyes of the opposing powers of Hades as they heard thunderous shouts and armies giving commands and saying: “Lift up the gates, O you rulers of yours!” Not “open” them, but lift them up from their very foundations, uproot them, remove them, so that they may never be shut again. “Lift up the gates, O you rulers of yours!” This is not because the Master who is present lacks the power to enter through shut doors when he gives the command. Rather, he is leaving to you, as to runaway slaves, the work of lifting up, removing and smashing the everlasting gates. That is why he gives the command not to your peoples but to the very ones who seem to be your rulers, saying: “Lift up the gates, O you rulers of yours.” Yours, and not anyone else's. Rulers, for the moment. For until now you have ruled wickedly over those who have slept from the beginning of the ages. From now on, though, you will no longer be their rulers, nor anyone else's. You will be rulers only of yourselves, and in the end not even of yourselves. For Christ, the heavenly door, is here. Make a way for him who rides over the western darkness of Hades. The Lord is his name, and to the Lord, the Lord, belong the ways out through the gates of death. You made the ways in; he has come to make the ways out. So do not delay. Lift up the gates, and be quick; lift them up, and do not put it off. But if you think you can wait, we command the gates themselves to be lifted up without hands, of their own accord. “And be lifted up, you everlasting gates!” In the same instant the powers cried out, the gates were lifted up, the chains were loosed, the bars were broken, the bolts fell out, the foundations of the prison were shaken, and the opposing powers were turned to flight. One shoved another, one tripped over another, one shouted to another to run. They shuddered, they were shaken, they were stunned, they were thrown into confusion, they were changed, they were terrified. They stood still and at the same time were beside themselves; they were at a loss and at the same time [Marginal notes: variant reading “darkening”; variant reading “having filled”; Gen. 43.]

they trembled. One stood gaping, while another hid his face against his knees. Another froze face down, another was turned to stone as if dead, another was gripped by amazement, another lay there [heavenly?] transformed, and another fled further inside. For there Christ then pierced the heads of the mighty in their bewilderment; there they were shaken by him; there they loosed their bridles and said: “Who is this King of glory? Who is this, so great, who with such hosts works such wonders here? Who is this King of glory, who is now doing in Hades things that never before happened in Hades? Who is this who is leading out from here those who have slept from the beginning of the ages? Who is this who has loosed and destroyed the boldness and might of us, the unconquered, and is leading out of the prison of Hades those fettered from the beginning of the ages?” The Master's powers cried out to them, saying: “Do you want to learn, you lawless tyrants, who this King of glory is? The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord, mighty and powerful and invincible in battle. This is the one who drove you out and hurled you down from the vaults of heaven, you wretched and lawless tyrants! This is the one who crushed the heads of your dragons in the waters of the Jordan. This is the one who through the cross made a public example of you, triumphed over you and put you to death. This is the one who bound you, plunged you into darkness and sent you down to the abyss. This is the one who is sending you to eternal fire and Gehenna and is destroying you. So do not delay and do not wait. Hurry and bring out the prisoners whom you have wickedly oppressed until now. For your might has now been destroyed; your tyranny has now come to an end; your insolence has been dreadfully brought to nothing; your boasting has utterly failed; your strength has been trampled down and has perished.” This is what the Master's own powers said to the opposing powers, and as they spoke they pressed on. Some razed the prison from its very foundations; others pursued the opposing authorities as they fled from the outer chambers further inside. Others searched the hiding places, the strongholds and the caves, and [?]. Others brought prisoners to the Master, one from here and another from there. Others bound the tyrant in unbreakable bonds, while others released those bound from the beginning of the ages. Some gave orders and others carried them out with all speed. Some ran ahead as the Master went further in, while others followed him as their King and victorious God. All this, and more than this, was being done and proclaimed in Hades, and everything was in uproar and shaking. The coming of the Master was about to reach the lowest of the lowest depths, and that Adam, the first of all human beings to be created, [Marginal notes: variant reading “was frozen”; F. “who is this”; “in it”; variant reading “destroyed”; variant reading “things”; variant reading “has been loosed”.]

the first to be formed and the first to die, was held captive further inside than all the rest, under heavy guard. He heard the footsteps of the Master as he came in to the prisoners, and he recognized his voice as he walked about in the prison. Turning to all those who had been imprisoned with him from the beginning of the ages, he said: “I hear the sound of someone's footsteps coming toward us. If he has indeed seen fit to come here, we are freed from our bonds; if we do indeed see him with us, we are redeemed from Hades.” As Adam was saying these and similar things to all who had been condemned with him, the Master came in to them, holding the victorious weapon of the cross. When Adam, the first to be formed, saw him, he struck his breast in astonishment and cried out to them all, saying: “My Lord be with all!” And Christ answered Adam: “And with your spirit.” Taking him by the hand, he raised him up, saying: “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you. I am your God, who for your sake became your son. For you and for those descended from you I now speak, and with authority I command those in bonds: ‘Come out!’ and those in darkness: ‘Be enlightened!’ and those who are asleep: ‘Arise!’ To you I give this command: Awake, O sleeper! For I did not make you so that you would be held captive in Hades. Arise from the dead: I am the life of the dead. Arise, work of my hands; arise, my likeness, you who were made in my image. Awake, let us go from here. For you are in me and I am in you; together we are one undivided person. For your sake I, your God, became your son. For your sake I, the Master, took your form, the form of a slave. For your sake I, who am above the heavens, came upon the earth and beneath the earth. For your sake, for humankind, I became like a man without help, free among the dead. For your sake, who went out from a garden, I was handed over to the Jews from a garden and was crucified in a garden. See the spittle on my face, which I accepted for your sake to restore you to the breath first breathed into you. See the blows on my cheeks, which I accepted to restore your distorted form to my image. See the scourging on my back, which I accepted to scatter the burden of your sins that lay upon your back. See my hands, nailed to the tree for good, for the sake of you who once wickedly stretched out your hand to the tree. See my feet, nailed and pierced to the tree, for the sake of your feet, which wickedly ran to the tree of disobedience. On the sixth day the sentence was passed [?], and I have labored to form you anew and to open paradise. For your sake I tasted gall, to heal you of the bitter pleasure of that sweet food. I tasted vinegar, to abolish the sharpness of your death and the unnatural cup you drank. I accepted [Marginal notes: variant reading “lying”; variant reading “lying”; variant reading “on which the ancient transgression took place, on the sixth day, and your forming in paradise”.]

a sponge, to wipe out the record of your sin. I accepted a reed, to sign the decree of freedom for the human race. I slept on the cross, and my side was pierced with a spear, for the sake of you who slept in paradise and brought Eve out of your side. My side has healed the pain of your side. My sleep will bring you out of the sleep of Hades. My spear has halted the sword that was turned against you. So awake, let us go from here. The enemy brought you out of the land of paradise; I am restoring you no longer to paradise but to a heavenly throne. I kept you from the tree that was a figure of life, but see, I myself, who am life, am united with you. I set the cherubim to guard you as a slave; I now make the cherubim worship you as God. You hid from God because you were naked; but see, you have hidden God within yourself, naked. You were clothed in the garment of skin, the garment of shame; but I, though I am God, have clothed myself in the garment of your flesh and blood. So arise, let us go from here: from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, from darkness to eternal light. Arise, let us go from here: from pain to gladness, from slavery to freedom, from prison to the Jerusalem above, from bonds to rest, from captivity to the delight of paradise, from earth to heaven. For this is why I died and rose again, so that I might be Lord of both the dead and the living. Arise, let us go from here, for my heavenly Father is waiting for the lost sheep. The ninety-nine sheep, the angels, are waiting for their fellow servant Adam, to see when he will rise, when he will go up and return to God. The throne of the cherubim is made ready; those who will carry you up are swift and ready; the bridal chamber is prepared; the feast is ready; the eternal tents and dwelling places are ready; the treasuries of good things have been opened; the kingdom of heaven has been prepared before the ages. What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered the human heart: these are the good things that await humankind.” As the Master was saying these and similar things, Adam, who was united with him, rose with him. Eve rose with him too, and many other bodies that had slept in faith from the beginning of the ages arose, proclaiming the Master's three-day [?]
